paragraphs: Swamiji drew this tale from the ancient Chandogya Upanishad. Its telling is simple, even rough, he said, but it carries a deep principle about how knowledge comes to a seeker.

A young boy named Satyakama wanted to study the Vedas. He asked his mother for his father's name and his caste, since a teacher would surely want to know. His mother, Jabala, had never been married, and in those days such a child was shunned by society and barred from sacred study. Honestly, she told him she did not know who his father was; she had worked as a servant in many homes. All she could give him was her name, Jabala, and his, Satyakama.

The boy went to a sage and asked to become his student. When the sage asked about his father and caste, Satyakama repeated exactly what his mother had said. The sage was moved. Only a true Brahmin, he declared, would speak so honestly about something so painful. Because the boy had not strayed from the truth, the sage accepted him.

Then came a most unusual education. The teacher handed Satyakama four hundred thin, weak cows and sent him into the forest, telling him to return only when the herd had grown to a thousand. Years passed. One day a great bull in the herd spoke up: they were now a thousand, it said, time to go home, and it offered to teach him something of Brahman. The four directions, it explained, are parts of the Lord. Then it said the fire would teach him more.

Each evening on the journey back, as Satyakama lit the sacred fire and made his offering, a new teacher appeared. The fire spoke of earth, sky, heaven and ocean as portions of Brahman. A swan told him the fire, sun, moon and lightning were parts of It. A bird called Madgu taught that breath, sight, hearing and mind belonged to It too.

When Satyakama finally reached his teacher, the sage saw at once that the boy's face glowed like one who knows Brahman, and asked who had taught him. "Beings other than men," Satyakama replied, yet he still asked his Guru to instruct him. So the sage taught him everything he himself had learned, leaving nothing out.
learn: Satyakama's honesty about an uncomfortable background opened the door his circumstances seemed to close. And once he was sincere and patient, even ordinary work like caring for cattle became a classroom. Truthfulness and steady effort turn everyday life into learning.
